This pedal can be powered by a Dunlop ECB003 9-volt adapter, or the DC Brick™, Iso-Brick™, and Mini Iso-Brick™ power supplies (not included). Warranty Information The Long Story The MXR Sugar Drive Pedal provides a diverse range of clear and transparent overdrive tones, from sauced up boosting to blown-tube distortion. It's based on a rare overdrive pedal that has acquired a mythical reputation among fanatical tone-seekers thanks to its unique circuit design. The key elements of that circuit design are the Drive control and something called a voltage doubler. First, the Drive control on this pedal doesn't just increase the intensity of the overdrive pedal. It starts with your clean signal and then blends it with the overdrive effect as you turn it up, replicating the smooth transition of an amplifier going from clean to dirty. The voltage doubler increases overall headroom, which opens everything up nicely. Of course, we had to put the MXR touch on this circuit. If you're all about true bypass, then you're in luck—this pedal uses it by default. The original used buffered bypass, though, and we know there's a lot of players out there who don't want to fix something that isn't broken. They're in luck, too—just flick the Buffer switch on the side of the pedal to enable buffered bypassing. With a simple three-knob setup and an MXR mini housing, this is the go-to overdrive to have on your pedalboard. It's versatile and it saves space, and unlike the original pedals it's based on, it won't cost you thousands of dollars. Product Demo In The News MXR® CARBON COPY® MINI ANALOG DELAY: A little delay. sources.h1: Video Mxr Sugar Drive Review: A Practical Guide to Its 90s Classic Overdrive Sound
sources.excerpt: Video Mxr Sugar Drive Review: A Practical Guide to Its 90s Classic Overdrive Sound | GearStrings GEARSTRINGS Home Blog Categories Authors About Home / Blog / guitars guitars Video Mxr Sugar Drive Review: A Practical Guide to Its 90s Classic Overdrive Sound By zoe-langford June 10, 2026 Video Mxr Sugar Drive Review: A Practical Guide to Its 90s Classic Overdrive Sound The Video Mxr Sugar Drive delivers a faithful, responsive reinterpretation of the mid-90s transparent overdrive pedal—think the early-’90s Ibanez Tube Screamer variants and modified Boss SD-1 circuits—but with tighter low-end control, improved headroom, and a more dynamic response to guitar volume and picking intensity. For guitarists seeking authentic 90s alternative rock, grunge, or indie pop drive without excessive compression or muddiness, this pedal works especially well with passive single-coils into clean-to-breakup tube amps. It is not a high-gain distortion unit; it excels when used as a boost-into-preamp or subtle saturation layer—not as a standalone heavy distortion source. 🎸 If your goal is nuanced, touch-sensitive overdrive that cleans up cleanly when rolling back pickup volume—especially on Stratocasters, Telecasters, or P-90-equipped guitars—the Sugar Drive warrants serious audition alongside other mid-gain overdrives. About Video Mxr Releases The Sugar Drive Its Take On A 90s Classic Video Mxr is a small-batch US-based effects builder known for meticulous circuit analysis, hand-soldered construction, and tonal fidelity over novelty. Their Sugar Drive emerged in late 2022 as a direct response to player demand for a modernized version of the "90s garage-band overdrive"—a sonic archetype defined by modest gain (12–22 dB), asymmetrical clipping, soft compression, and a pronounced mid-hump centered around 700 Hz–1.2 kHz. Unlike many reissues, Video Mxr did not clone a single pedal. Instead, they reverse-engineered several vintage-labeled SD-1 variants (notably ’93–’97 Japanese PCB revisions), early TS9 derivatives used by Pacific Northwest bands, and modified MXR Dyna Comp + OD hybrids heard on albums like *Nevermind* and *Siamese Dream*. The result is a discrete-component, Class-A biased op-amp design using JRC4558D and TL072 ICs, with a dual-stage clipping topology (silicon diodes + LED soft-clipping) and a buffered bypass that preserves high-end integrity over long cable runs. What distinguishes it from generic boutique clones is its attention to transient response: the input stage features a low-noise FET buffer that maintains string attack and pick definition even at higher drive settings—a key differentiator from vintage-correct designs that compress transients more aggressively. The pedal ships with a 9V DC center-negative power supply, true-bypass toggle switch, and compact aluminum enclosure (118 × 68 × 50 mm). No battery option is included, consistent with Video Mxr’s reliability-first ethos. Why This Matters: Benefits for Tone, Playability, and Knowledge Guitarists often conflate “90s overdrive” with generic midrange boost or muddy breakup. In reality, the defining characteristic of that era’s most-used drives was dynamic interaction : how cleanly the pedal responded to guitar volume changes, how naturally it blended with amp overdrive, and how transparently it preserved EQ character downstream. The Sugar Drive makes these behaviors explicit—and teachable. For tone: Its midrange lift is surgical, not broad. It avoids the nasal 1.5 kHz spike of later TS9 reissues and instead emphasizes the fundamental-rich 850 Hz region where neck-position humbuckers and bridge-position single-coils converge. This allows chords to retain clarity while solos cut through dense mixes—critical for recording layered guitar parts or playing in loud band contexts. For playability: The Drive knob offers logarithmic taper and calibrated resistance, giving precise control between 10% (barely-there boost) and 75% (warm, singing sustain with minimal splatter).
